stories.title: Christians in India fear that tighter laws target them
stories.summary: Maharashtra is the 13th Indian state of 28 to enact an anti-conversion law.
article_sentences: Those going to church next Sunday in Mumbai will take part in an uneasy new ritual before the service.
They will sign a form declaring that they are attending the service voluntarily and are not being forced to go to church or convert to Christianity.

Around 4,000 churches in the Mumbai Metropolitan Area in the western Indian state of Maharashtra have decided to collect such “consent forms” to protect themselves ahead of an upcoming anti-conversion law that criminalises alleged forced conversions.

“These consent forms are the least safety measure we can take to protect us from legal proceedings if anyone attempts to accuse the pastors or churches of forcibly converting people,” Dolphy D’souza, spokesperson for the Bombay Catholic Society, told.
“There have been a dozen disruptions of prayers in the past six months, by Hindu right-wing groups under the pretext of exposing forced conversions.
So we have also asked churches to install CCTV cameras to identify attackers,” he added.

The defensive actions in Mumbai are the latest response to a range of allegedly discriminatory actions by the Indian government against the Christian community, which is the third-largest religious group in India and comprises 2.3 per cent of the population.

These include anti-conversion laws in several states and the tightening of laws governing foreign funding of non-profits, which could result in the seizure of assets such as schools and hospitals built with such donations.

Representatives of the Christian community in Mumbai said they fear an uptick in vigilante attacks on churches from Aug 28, when Maharashtra’s anti-conversion law, the Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act 2026, comes into force.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in the western state passed the law in July.
With that, Maharashtra becomes the 13th Indian state of 28 to enact an anti-conversion law.
